Right, the cycle alone needs 5.833. The value does not depend on the start node; smaller is better connected." width="100%"} The Kemeny constant is the expected number of steps a random walk needs to reach a target node chosen at random from the walk's stationary distribution. Remarkably, it does not depend on where the walk starts. It measures how quickly the network can be navigated or mixed as a whole: smaller is better connected. It is computed from the spectrum as `Σ_{i≥2} 1 / (1 - λ_i)`, over all but the largest eigenvalue of the normalized adjacency `D^-½ A D^-½`, and matches NetworkX's `kemeny_constant()`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether the walk follows edge weights. If `None` (default), follows the graph. Weights must be non-negative. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The Kemeny constant. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is directed, empty or disconnected, or has a negative weight. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} A complete graph is navigated faster than a cycle of the same size: ::: {#d407a4a8 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec complete = ec.Graph().add_full_graph(6).kemeny_constant() cycle = ec.Graph().add_cycle_graph(6).kemeny_constant() round(complete, 3), round(cycle, 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (4.167, 5.833) ``` ::: :::
